newsitem.title: CHINA: HK dollar seen coming under renewed pressure.
newsitem.headline: HK dollar seen coming under renewed pressure.

text.p: The Hong Kong dollar is likely to come under renewed speculative pressure during the coming week but no dramatic fall is expected, analysts said on Sunday.
"I think some pressure may be building but at the present time I don't see any way that Hong Kong would abandon its peg (to the U.S. dollar)," investment adviser Marc Faber said.
"For the time being, it's safe," he added.
The Hong Kong dollar, the last major Asian currency linked to the U.S. dollar, has been pegged at HK$7.8 to US$1.00 since 1983 but it has traded at around 7.74 this year.
"We have a peg here basically. So it may weaken a little bit, but not much," Faber said.

Analysts said the local currency would face continued attacks during the week after it fell to around the key support level of 7.75 to the dollar on Friday. Hong Kong markets are closed on Monday for a public holiday.
Asian currencies, which have been hit recently by a spate of speculative attacks, slid on Friday after Indonesia's decision to move to a managed float system for the rupiah.
"The market seems to be targeting the Hong Kong dollar as the last peg left in Asia," a dealer at an Australian bank in London said.

Faber said investors may sell Hong Kong dollars for the U.S. dollar. Other foreign currency analysts said investors may switch from the Hong Kong dollar to Asian currencies, which have fallen sharply recently and may appear to be better bargains.
But market analysts in general foresaw no major fall in the Hong Kong dollar, tipping it to challenge the 7.6 level at the lowest.
Speculators believe the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the de facto central bank, is determined to control the local dollar rate at no lower than 7.75, a currency dealer said.
"We are confident the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) can safeguard the value of the Hong Kong dollar," Banking Association acting chairman Or Ching-fai told the Hong Kong Standard.
"The fundamentals of Hong Kong's economy are sound and healthy and we have a huge Exchange Fund," he said.
Hong Kong's exchange fund, reserves held to back the local dollar, stood at HK$569 billion at June 30 and foreign currency reserves amounted to US$82 billion.
The territory has made a contribution of US$1 billion from the exchange fund to the US$16 billion rescue package for Thailand organised by the International Monetary Fund.
Faber said he believed the HKMA, the de facto central bank, will keep the dollar peg at present.

Secretary for Financial Services Rafael Hui said the HKMA would remain vigilant to combat speculation against the Hong Kong dollar and speculators would not succeed in breaking the currency's peg to the U.S. dollar.
"I think the (HKMA) has been rather vigilant since the episode began, which was some weeks ago with the Thai baht," he told the South China Morning Post on Sunday.
"Other people should know better but obviously they don't. They have been burned before and I see no reason why they will not be again," he said.
Last week Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said that the government had spent US$1.0 billion defending the local currency on a single day in July.
